set.seed(60203)
repetitions <- 5000L
sample_sizes <- c(5L, 30L, 100L)
sampling_means <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  data.frame(
    Sample_size = factor(n, levels = sample_sizes),
    Sample_mean = replicate(repetitions, mean(rexp(n, rate = 1 / 10)))
  )
}))
sampling_split <- split(sampling_means$Sample_mean, sampling_means$Sample_size)
sampling_summary <- data.frame(
  n = sample_sizes,
  Mean_of_means = vapply(sampling_split, mean, numeric(1)),
  Empirical_SE = vapply(sampling_split, sd, numeric(1)),
  Model_SE = 10 / sqrt(sample_sizes),
  row.names = NULL
)

::: {.callout-note title="Chapter overview"}

Chapter 1 explained what study observations represent and how they
arise. This chapter develops their descriptive use: how to read the
recorded data and turn measurements into useful displays and summaries.
Its small invented examples make the arithmetic visible before we
return to a larger school dataset. A final simulation extends the same
ideas of center, spread, and shape to summaries from repeated samples,
preparing us to understand statistical uncertainty.

By the end of the chapter you will be able to read a dataset as cases,
variables, and values, recognize long and wide layouts, and identify
the denominator and sample-selection procedure; see and summarize one
distribution by shape, center, and spread; compare groups while keeping
their variation visible; connect variable forms to probability models,
calculate transformations and Normal areas, and describe a relationship
with a graph, covariance, correlation and linear adjustment; interpret
each description within its study setting;
explain what a sampling distribution and standard error show about
repeated samples; and distinguish one sample's sampling error from
that distribution and its standard error.
:::

## Understanding the Dataset

Chapter 1 connected study units and measurement procedures to the
observations available for analysis. Here we examine the resulting
records: how observations are arranged, what scales and codes mean,
and which cases and denominator support each summary. These details
turn the study's account of its evidence into data we can describe.

Schools often want to know whether students with more absences tend to
receive lower grades. Before choosing a statistical method, it helps to
see what information is actually available.

Our main example uses the mathematics dataset from Cortez and Silva's
student-performance study, based on school reports and questionnaires
from two Portuguese secondary schools [@cortez2008using; @cortez2008data].
It contains data for **395 students**, including their absence counts and
final mathematics grades. The repository also provides a separate
Portuguese-language dataset; the calculations here use the mathematics
data.

We will ask: **Among these 395 students, how do recorded absences and final
mathematics grades vary together?** To answer, we first describe grades
on their own, then compare groups and examine relationships. We put that
description back into its school setting before asking a related question:
how could a summary change if we observed a different sample?

### Cases, variables, values, and data layout

A **dataset** brings together information about people, objects, or
measurement occasions. A **case** is the entity or occasion being
described. In this dataset each case is one student. A **variable** is a
feature that can differ across students, such as absences or final grade;
a **value** is the measurement or category for a particular student.

@tbl-student-preview shows six selected students. The student IDs are
labels added for this tutorial. School codes GP and MS identify the two
schools. Reading across U001's row gives six absences and a final grade
of six: the same numeral for two different measurements, a count and a
score. Reading down the Absences column compares that count across
students. The identifier keeps the two measurements linked to the
student they describe.

```{=latex}

```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-student-preview

preview <- students[c(1, 2, 3, 350, 351, 352),
                    c("student_id", "school", "absences", "final_grade")]
names(preview) <- c("Student ID", "School", "Absences", "Final grade")
knitr::kable(preview, booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE,
             align = c("l", "l", "r", "r"))
```

The two numerical columns can also be written as a **data matrix**,
with one row for each displayed student and one column for each variable.
Let $x_{ij}$ denote the entry in row $i$ and column $j$: here $j=1$
means absences and $j=2$ final grade. The first index numbers these six
displayed rows, rather than their positions in the original dataset.
Thus $x_{31}=10$ absences and $x_{42}=13$ grade points.

$$
\mathbf X=(x_{ij})=
\begin{pmatrix}6&6\\4&6\\10&10\\10&13\\8&8\\2&13\end{pmatrix},
\qquad i=1,\ldots,6,\quad j=1,2.
$$

Each column can be summarized separately. The symbol $\sum$ means to
add the indicated entries. For example, the sum for the first column is
$\sum_{i=1}^6 x_{i1}=6+4+10+10+8+2=40$, so its mean is
$40/6=6.6667$ absences. The grade column has mean $56/6=9.3333$
grade points. These summarize the six displayed cases; the later
summaries use all 395 students. In general, for $n$ rows,

$$
\bar x_j=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij},\qquad
s_j^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)^2.
$$

The first formula gives a column's mean. The second gives its sample
variance, developed through a small calculation in Section 2.2. This
notation organizes numerical entries; identifiers and school labels
still have their own meanings and are not quantities to average.
For two named variables we can write $x_i=x_{i1}$ and $y_i=x_{i2}$.
Subscripts have locally stated meanings: an index for a column here
can have a different declared use in a later grouped-data calculation.

Chapter 1 distinguished the units a study observes from the occasions
on which they are measured. We can recognize that connection in a
dataset's arrangement. Suppose a separate, invented study records a
score for each of 120 students at the beginning and end of a term,
with both scores observed for every student. There are 120 students
and 240 measurement occasions. In a **long layout**, each row describes
one student on one occasion; an occasion column identifies when the
score was recorded. In a **wide layout**, each row describes one
student, and separate columns hold the beginning and end scores.
@tbl-ch02-layout-long and @tbl-ch02-layout-wide show the same six
invented scores for three of the students.

| Student ID | Beginning score | End score |
